In managed control planes the provider manages etcd. You can verify desired state with kubectl get <resource> or inspect etcd with etcdctl when you control the datastore.

questions.category: Kubernetes — What Happens Behind the Scenes
questions.question: What does the Deployment Controller do?
questions.answer: The Deployment controller watches Deployment objects in the API server and continuously reconciles their .spec with cluster state by creating/updating ReplicaSets and their Pods to match the desired PodTemplate, replica count, and update strategy. For rolling updates it creates a new ReplicaSet (with a pod-template-hash), scales up the new RS and scales down old RSes according to maxSurge/maxUnavailable, and records revision history (subject to revisionHistoryLimit) so rollbacks (kubectl rollout undo) are possible. It also observes progressDeadlineSeconds and sets Deployment conditions; verify with kubectl get deployment/my-deploy -o yaml, kubectl rollout status, kubectl rollout history, and kubectl describe deployment.

questions.category: Kubernetes — What Happens Behind the Scenes
questions.question: What does the ReplicaSet Controller do?
questions.answer: A ReplicaSet controller continuously reconciles a ReplicaSet object's spec.replicas by creating or deleting Pods that match its label selector so the actual state equals the desired state. It watches ReplicaSet and Pod resources via the kube-apiserver, enqueues events to the controller-manager workqueue, and in each reconcile loop compares status.replicas/availableReplicas to spec.replicas, creating Pods from the ReplicaSet’s podTemplate or deleting excess Pods. ReplicaSets set ownerReferences on Pods (preventing orphans) and support adoption of matching Pods. Verify with kubectl get rs, kubectl describe rs <name> (shows events, status) and kubectl scale rs/<name> --replicas=N to observe pod creation/deletion.

questions.category: Kubernetes — What Happens Behind the Scenes
questions.question: Who creates the Pods?
questions.answer: Pods are created either by API clients (kubectl, client-go) submitting Pod objects to the kube-apiserver or by Kubernetes controllers that create Pod objects via the controller manager (Deployments → ReplicaSets → Pods, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs/CronJobs). The scheduler binds a Pending Pod to a node, and the kubelet on that node starts containers via the container runtime. The kubelet also creates static pods by reading manifests from its --pod-manifest-path and will publish mirror Pods to the API server. Verify ownership with kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml and inspect metadata.ownerReferences or kubectl describe pod which shows “Controlled By”.

questions.category: Kubernetes — What Happens Behind the Scenes
questions.question: What does kube-scheduler do?
questions.answer: kube-scheduler watches the API server for unscheduled Pods, evaluates cluster state from its informer/cache and the Node objects, and selects a target Node that satisfies predicates (resources, nodeSelector, taints/tolerations, nodeAffinity, PodTopologySpread, etc.) and scoring policies. The scheduler runs the scheduling framework plugins (PreFilter/Filter/Score/Reserve/Permit/Bind/PostBind) and then binds the Pod by writing pod.spec.nodeName or using the Binding subresource, creating a "Scheduled" event. It supports extenders, multiple profiles, leader election for HA, and handles retries/backoff on failures. Verify operation with kubectl describe pod (shows "Scheduled to <node>") or kubectl get pods -o wide to see the node assignment.

questions.category: Kubernetes — What Happens Behind the Scenes
questions.question: How does the scheduler decide which node should run a Pod?
questions.answer: The kube-scheduler watches unscheduled Pods via informers, builds feasible nodes using the scheduling framework plugins (PreFilter/Filter) — e.g., NodeResourcesFit, TaintToleration, NodeAffinity, PodTopologySpread — then scores remaining nodes (Score phase) using configured scoring plugins to produce a rank. After Score, the highest-scoring node is selected, the scheduler Reserve/Permit/PreBind hooks run, and the scheduler issues a Bind API call (POST /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}/pods/{name}/binding) to set the Pod’s node assignment. You can verify decisions with kubectl describe pod (scheduling events) and kube-scheduler logs (kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/kube-scheduler) and inspect scheduling cache via metrics and scheduler profile configuration.

questions.category: Kubernetes — What Happens Behind the Scenes
questions.question: What does kubelet do?
questions.answer: kubelet is the primary Kubernetes node agent that watches the API server for PodSpecs assigned to its Node and ensures the containers described are running. It communicates with the container runtime via the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) (e.g., containerd, cri-o) to pull images, create/kill containers and mount volumes, and it enforces cgroups/resource limits. Kubelet executes liveness/readiness/startup probes, manages secrets/configMaps, performs certificate rotation, and evicts pods under resource pressure. It reports NodeStatus and PodStatus (and updates NodeLease heartbeats) to the API server and exposes /metrics and /healthz for scraping; verify with kubectl describe node, kubectl get pods -o wide, or systemctl status kubelet.

questions.category: Kubernetes — What Happens Behind the Scenes
questions.question: What role does containerd/the container runtime play?
questions.answer: containerd is the cluster’s container runtime: it stores and serves container images, manages snapshots, and creates/runs OCI containers at the request of the kubelet via the CRI (Container Runtime Interface). Kubelet talks to containerd over a gRPC socket (e.g. /run/containerd/containerd.sock or via the containerd CRI plugin) issuing PullImage, CreateContainer, StartContainer, StopContainer, and RemoveContainer. containerd manages image content, snapshotters, and delegates low-level process setup to containerd-shim + an OCI runtime like runc for namespaces and cgroups. Operators verify behavior with systemctl status containerd, ss -ltnp | grep containerd, ctr images ls, ctr containers ls or crictl ps/images when using the CRI shim.

questions.category: Kubernetes — What Happens Behind the Scenes
questions.question: What is the Kubernetes reconciliation loop?
questions.answer: The reconciliation loop is the controller pattern where a controller continuously compares the desired state (object.spec) with the current state (cluster resources) and takes operations to converge them. Controllers watch the API server (via informers/reflectors and watches), enqueue keys in a workqueue, and run a sync handler that reads the latest object (resourceVersion), computes a patch, then calls the API (PATCH/PUT) or creates/deletes sub-resources and updates status. Retries, RateLimiter backoff, requeue-on-error, and optimistic concurrency using resourceVersion handle transient failure and races. Verify behavior with live tools: kubectl get <kind> <name> -o yaml, kubectl get events, kubectl get <kind> -w, and inspect controller logs (kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-controller-manager).

questions.category: Kubernetes — What Happens Behind the Scenes
questions.question: Does a Deployment directly create containers?
questions.answer: No. A Deployment (apps/v1) is a declarative controller that creates or updates ReplicaSet objects; those ReplicaSets in turn create Pods. The Deployment controller in kube-controller-manager manipulates ReplicaSet.spec.template; the ReplicaSet controller observes that ReplicaSet and creates Pods whose metadata.ownerReferences points to the ReplicaSet. The kubelet then instructs the container runtime (via the CRI such as containerd) to create the containers specified in each PodSpec. Verify with kubectl: kubectl get deployment, kubectl get rs, kubectl get pods and kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml to see ownerReferences linking Pod → ReplicaSet and kubectl describe rs to inspect the template.

questions.question: How do you manage secrets in AKS?
questions.answer: Use a centralized secret store (Azure Key Vault or HashiCorp Vault) and avoid baking secrets into images or long-lived Kubernetes secrets. Example flow with Key Vault + CSI driver + Workload Identity: create vault and secret: az keyvault create -n myVault -g myRG; az keyvault secret set --vault-name myVault -n db-pass --value "s3cr3t". Install CSI driver and Azure provider: helm repo add secrets-store-csi-driver https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/secrets-store-csi-driver && helm install csi secrets-store-csi-driver/secrets-store-csi-driver; helm install provider-azure https://github.com/Azure/secrets-store-csi-driver-provider-azure/releases. Enable Azure AD Workload Identity (create federated credential via az ad app federated-credential create) and mount secrets via a Pod spec with volume driver secrets-store.csi.k8s.io. Verify with kubectl describe pod and check mounted file inside container or kubectl get secret if using secret sync. Configure RBAC, Key Vault access policies or RBAC roles, and rotate via Key Vault versions.

questions.question: Why shouldn’t production secrets be stored directly in Kubernetes YAML or Git?
questions.answer: Storing production secrets directly in Kubernetes YAML or Git exposes them to broad, persistent attack surfaces: Git preserves history and forks (so leaked values remain retrievable), CI/CD logs and backups may capture them, and repo access often has wider distribution than runtime secret access. Kubernetes Secret objects are only base64-encoded (viewable with kubectl get secret -o yaml) unless you enable kube-apiserver encryption-at-rest via --encryption-provider-config and a KMS provider. Best practice is to use an external secret store (HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault) or tooling like SealedSecrets/External Secrets, enforce scanning (git-secrets), and verify with kubectl that runtime secrets aren’t exposed in YAML or git history.

questions.question: How would you integrate Azure Key Vault with AKS?
questions.answer:
Use the Secrets Store CSI driver with the Azure Key Vault provider and Azure AD workload identity (recommended). Install the CSI driver and Azure provider via Helm:
- helm repo add secrets-store-csi-driver https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/secrets-store-csi-driver/charts
- helm repo add csi-secrets-store-provider-azure https://azure.github.io/secrets-store-csi-driver-provider-azure/charts
- helm install csi secrets-store-csi-driver/secrets-store-csi-driver --namespace kube-system
- helm install csi-azure csi-secrets-store-provider-azure/secrets-store-csi-driver-provider-azure --namespace kube-system

Create an AAD app / managed identity and a federated credential (az ad app federated-credential create) then annotate a Kubernetes service account for workload identity. Define a SecretProviderClass referencing your Key Vault secret(s), mount it into pods, and optionally sync to Kubernetes Secrets. Verify with kubectl apply -f secretproviderclass.yaml, kubectl get pods, kubectl describe pod, and kubectl get secret <name> -n <ns>.

questions.question: What is the Azure Key Vault Provider for Secrets Store CSI Driver?
questions.answer: The Azure Key Vault Provider for the Secrets Store CSI Driver is an open-source CSI provider that lets Kubernetes pods mount Azure Key Vault secrets, keys, and certificates as files (under /mnt/secrets-store) or sync them into Kubernetes Secret objects. It uses Azure AD authentication (user-assigned/managed identity or service principal) and is configured via the SecretProviderClass CRD. Install the CSI driver and provider with Helm (examples: helm repo add secrets-store-csi-driver https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/secrets-store-csi-driver/charts; helm install secrets-store-csi-driver secrets-store-csi-driver/secrets-store-csi-driver -n kube-system; helm repo add csi-secrets-store-provider-azure https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Azure/secrets-store-csi-driver-provider-azure/master/charts; helm install csi-secrets-store-provider-azure csi-secrets-store-provider-azure/csi-secrets-store-provider-azure -n kube-system). Verify by creating a SecretProviderClass, launching a pod, then checking mounted files at /mnt/secrets-store and optionally kubectl get secret <name>.

questions.question: How can an AKS Pod authenticate to Azure Key Vault?
questions.answer: Use Azure AD Workload Identity (recommended) or the older aad-pod-identity. With Workload Identity: 1) Register an Azure AD app (service principal) and create a federated credential that trusts the AKS OIDC issuer and the Kubernetes service account subject (az ad app federated-credential create --id <appId> --parameters ...). 2) Grant that app Key Vault access via Key Vault RBAC (az role assignment create --assignee <appId> --role "Key Vault Secrets User" --scope /subscriptions/.../resourceGroups/.../providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/<vault>). 3) Annotate the k8s service account with azure.workload.identity/client-id=<appId> and mount the projected token; set AZURE_CLIENT_ID/AZURE_TENANT_ID and AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE in the pod. Use DefaultAzureCredential in SDKs or the Azure Key Vault REST API to GetSecret; verify by catting the token file in the pod and successfully calling the Key Vault secret endpoint.

questions.question: What is Microsoft Entra Workload ID?
questions.answer: Microsoft Entra Workload ID is Microsoft’s capability for managing non-human identities (workloads) — service principals, managed identities, and federated identities — enabling secure token-based authentication for applications, containers, and CI/CD without client secrets. It supports workload identity federation (OIDC) so external workloads exchange a short-lived token for an Azure AD access token. Operational commands: create a federated credential with az ad app federated-credential create --id <appId> --parameters @cred.json, inspect the service principal with az ad sp show --id <appId>, and request a token using the OAuth 2.0 JWT-bearer flow (grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer) against https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/oauth2/v2.0/token to verify issuance. This enables secretless, auditable workload authentication.

questions.question: Why is Workload Identity preferable to storing Azure credentials?
questions.answer: Workload Identity avoids embedding long‑lived Azure credentials in pods by federating Kubernetes service accounts to Azure AD and issuing short‑lived tokens. Benefits include no secret sprawl or manual rotation, least‑privilege via Azure RBAC on the federated identity, and auditable token issuance in Azure AD. In AKS you enable it with az aks update -g <rg> -n <cluster> --enable-workload-identity, create a K8s service account (kubectl create sa mysa) and annotate it (kubectl annotate sa mysa azure.workload.identity/client-id=<appId>), and create a federated credential (az ad app federated-credential create --id <appId> --parameters @params.json). Verify with kubectl describe sa mysa and az ad app federated-credential list --id <appId>.

questions.question: How would you implement secret rotation?
questions.answer: Use a secrets manager (Azure Key Vault or HashiCorp Vault), mount secrets into AKS via the Secrets Store CSI driver (provider-azure or provider-vault) and enable automatic refresh. Example flow for Key Vault: az keyvault secret set --vault-name mykv --name db-password --value "new"; use a SecretProviderClass that sets rotationPollInterval (e.g., "60s") so the CSI driver refreshes and, if configured, syncs to a Kubernetes Secret via secretObjects. Verify with az keyvault secret show --vault-name mykv --name db-password and kubectl get secret my-db-secret -o yaml or kubectl describe pod to see updated volume mounts. For Vault, update with vault kv put secret/app password=new and use vault-agent sidecar or CSI with lease/renew APIs (vault token lookup, vault lease revoke) to validate rotation and consumption.

questions.question: Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted simply because they’re Base64 encoded?
questions.answer: No — Base64 is only an encoding, not encryption. By default Kubernetes stores Secret values base64-encoded in etcd (kubectl get secret my-secret -o yaml shows base64 data), which provides no confidentiality. To encrypt at rest you must enable the API server EncryptionConfiguration (providers like aescbc, aescbc with kms-plugin, or the KMS provider) and restart kube-apiserver with --encryption-provider-config. Verify by reading etcd directly (etcdctl get /registry/secrets/<namespace>%2F<name> shows ciphertext) or by checking kube-apiserver --encryption-provider-config path and that GET on Secret still decodes for authenticated API clients. Only with a configured provider are secrets encrypted at rest.

questions.question: How would you restrict access to Kubernetes Secrets?
questions.answer: Use least-privilege RBAC + namespaces + service accounts: create a Role (verbs: get,list,watch) scoped to a namespace and bind only the specific ServiceAccount with RoleBinding, e.g. kubectl apply -f role.yaml and kubectl apply -f rolebinding.yaml; verify with kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n myns --as system:serviceaccount:myns:my-sa. Enable kube-apiserver secret encryption (EncryptionConfiguration with providers aescbc or KMS v1 plugin) so secrets are encrypted at rest; verify operator logs and KMS plugin health and that etcd-stored values are not plain plaintext. For cloud use the Secrets Store CSI driver (Azure Key Vault provider on AKS) to mount secrets into pods without creating Kubernetes Secrets and verify mounts inside the pod.

questions.category: Vertex AI, Cloud Security, and CSPM
questions.question: Can you walk me through the approach for securing a landing zone built on GCP?
questions.answer: Design using organization hierarchy, folders, and projects; enforce guardrails with Organization Policy (gcloud resource-manager org-policies list --organization=ORG_ID) and IAM least-privilege (gcloud projects get-iam-policy PROJECT_ID). Network isolation: use VPC Service Controls to create perimeters (gcloud access-context-manager perimeters create ...) and Private Service Connect for private access. Protect workloads with Binary Authorization, Shielded VMs, OS Login, and CMEK via Cloud KMS (gcloud kms keys versions list). Enable Cloud Audit Logs and send logs to a locked sink (gcloud logging sinks create) and enable Security Command Center and Cloud Asset Inventory to detect drift and risks (gcloud scc assets list / gcloud asset export). Verify posture with periodic exports (gcloud asset export) and automated scans from Security Command Center and CIS benchmarks.
