[RESULT] I’m aiming for a role where I can drive platform-level architecture, cloud security strategy, and production ML ops at scale.

questions.question: We are getting security alerts regarding vulnerabilities and CVEs. Can you walk me through your vulnerability management process?
questions.answer: Inventory: consolidate assets in CMDB and cloud APIs (AWS CLI `aws ec2 describe-instances`, GCP `gcloud compute instances list`, `kubectl get nodes`) and ingest software bill-of-materials. Discovery/scan: schedule authenticated scans with Tenable/Nessus, Qualys, and Snyk/Trivy for containers (`trivy image myrepo/app:latest`). Triage: correlate CVEs via NVD REST API (https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/1.0), evaluate CVSSv3, exploit maturity, and business impact. Remediate: prefer vendor patches/OS updates (`apt-get upgrade`, `yum update`), container rebuilds, or mitigations (WAF rules, firewall, feature flags). Deploy via standard pipelines and orchestration (`kubectl rollout restart deployment/my-app`) under change control. Verify by re-scanning and validating fixes (`nessus scan`, `trivy image`), track tickets in Jira and report MTTR and remediation rate.

questions.question: What would be your main KPI strategy for vulnerability management?
questions.answer: KPIs: 1) Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) by severity (Critical/High/Med/Low) measured as ticket close-time from scan detection timestamp. 2) Percent assets patched within SLA (e.g., 7/30/90 days) per severity. 3) Scan coverage: % of assets authenticated-scanned (Nessus/Tenable/Qualys) and % of hosts scanned in last 7 days. 4) False‑positive rate (triaged vs. reported). 5) Exploitable backlog: count of findings with confirmed public exploit. Operational verification: ingest scanner timestamps and UUIDs into ticketing via API (e.g., JIRA REST), compute MTTR from detection_timestamp to JIRA resolution, enforce re‑scan to verify closure, and run host checks (PowerShell Get-HotFix or rpm -q/<dpkg -l>) to confirm patch presence. These KPIs are tracked per asset group and reported weekly.

questions.question: How do you identify the actual risk exposure of a vulnerability?
questions.answer: Determine exposure by combining vulnerability data, asset context, and exploitability. Run a credentialed scanner (Nessus/OpenVAS/Qualys) to confirm vulnerability presence and configuration, e.g., Nessus scan results or Qualys API query showing vuln ID and last patch. Verify reachable service with nmap -sV <host> and confirm running version with curl or ssh. Check exploit availability (Exploit-DB, Metasploit module) and threat intel (CVE pages, vendor advisories). Assess compensating controls by querying EDR/SIEM (Splunk search for related Indicators of Compromise) and patch-management state. Estimate risk = likelihood (公网 exposure, exploit maturity, EDR gaps) × impact (asset criticality, data sensitivity), and validate by safely reproducing exploit in an isolated lab.

questions.question: Suppose a scan identifies more than 2,000 vulnerabilities. How would you prioritize, triage, and distribute them to the respective teams?
questions.answer:
First, deduplicate and normalize results (export CSV/JSON from the scanner), map vulnerabilities to assets and owners, and score by exploitable-first: exploit available/public exploit + CVSS >=7 + asset criticality. Apply SLAs: Critical (30 days or faster), High (60 days), Medium/Low by business risk. Automate ticket creation and assignment using the ticketing API; for example create JIRA issues via REST: 
curl -u user:token -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" https://jira.example.com/rest/api/2/issue -d '{"fields":{"project":{"key":"ENG"},"summary":"Remediate CVE-XXXX","description":"Scanner: Tenable; Asset: host.example; Fix: patch package","issuetype":{"name":"Task"}}}' 
Include remediation steps, rollback, test plan, and link scans. Verify fixes by rescanning (Nessus/Tenable/Qualys) and close tickets when the vuln is absent in the follow-up scan.

questions.question: If the same vulnerabilities keep appearing in an application after every release, how would you prevent their recurrence?
questions.answer: Perform root-cause analysis, enforce prevention in CI/CD, and verify with automated checks. Use git bisect/git blame to find when a vulnerability was introduced, add unit/regression tests and threat-model-derived acceptance tests, and integrate SAST/SCA/DAST into pipelines (e.g., sonar-scanner with SonarQube Quality Gate, trivy filesystem . or trivy image myapp:latest, OWASP ZAP baseline via zap-baseline.py). Configure the pipeline to fail on policy (non‑zero exit if Quality Gate fails or trivy returns findings with --severity HIGH,CRITICAL) and produce artifacts/SBOM for auditing. Track recurrence metrics (vulnerability recurrence rate, mean time to remediate) and verify by comparing successive scan reports to confirm the issue no longer reappears.

questions.question: How do you identify, validate, and handle a false positive in vulnerability management?
questions.answer: First, reproduce the finding: rerun the scan or targeted checks (e.g., Nessus/Qualys rescan) and perform active verification: nmap -sV -p <port> <host>, curl -I http://<host>:<port>, uname -a, dpkg -l | grep <package> or rpm -q <package>, and check /etc/os-release. Correlate with authoritative sources (NVD, vendor advisory) and search exploit databases (searchsploit CVE-YYYY-NNNN). If the issue cannot be reproduced and package/patch levels show no vulnerable version, mark as false positive in your ticketing system, add evidence, and suppress or whitelist the finding in the scanner using its suppression/exception feature, then schedule a targeted rescan to verify suppression and update asset inventory and runbooks.

questions.question: You have two vulnerabilities: one is Critical but not exploitable, while another is Medium but exploitable. Which one would you prioritize first, and why?
questions.answer: Prioritize the Medium but exploitable vulnerability first because risk = likelihood × impact; exploitability materially increases likelihood. Operationally: reproduce exploitability in an isolated lab (use Metasploit or vendor PoC) and confirm with authenticated scans (Nessus/Qualys) and host/process indicators. If confirmed, implement immediate mitigations — e.g., WAF rule, IPS signature, network segmentation, or temporary configuration change — then schedule a patch/change with a short SLA. For the Critical but currently non-exploitable issue, document the condition, proof that attack surface is unreachable (access controls, firewall rules), track with CVSS base + temporal notes, and schedule remediation per severity. Verify all remedial steps with rescans and ticketed evidence.

questions.question: How would you explain a critical security risk to a non-technical stakeholder?
questions.answer: This risk is like an unlocked exterior door: it lets attackers enter and access valuable assets. State the business impact (data loss, downtime, regulatory fines), likelihood (vulnerability exploitability, presence in internet-facing systems), and estimated cost if exploited. Recommend a prioritized, time-bound mitigation (patch, configuration change, WAF rule) with owner and SLA. Specify verification: scan with Qualys/Nessus or run `nmap -sV -p <port> <host>` and confirm patched software version with `dpkg -l`/`rpm -q` or `curl -I` to check headers. Report status on the risk dashboard and require closure criteria (proof of patch, successful rescans, and updated inventory).

questions.question: Explain the Secure Software Development Lifecycle and how security is integrated into it.
questions.answer: SSDLC embeds security across phases: requirements (security requirements, threat modeling using STRIDE/OWASP AMASS outputs), design (secure architecture, threat-model diagrams), implementation (secure coding standards, pre-commit hooks, code reviews, signed commits), testing (SAST e.g., bandit -r . for Python, gosec ./... for Go, SCA via snyk test or npm audit, DAST with OWASP ZAP, container scanning with trivy image <image> --exit-code 1), deployment (IaC scanning with checkov, policy-as-code enforcement in CI/CD), and maintenance (vulnerability management, CVE monitoring, regular patching). Integrate gates: CI fails on SAST/SCA/DAST findings, require MR approvals, pipeline artifacts scanned before release, and continuous monitoring in production.

questions.question: What is a Software Bill of Materials, and why is it useful?
questions.answer: A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is a machine-readable inventory listing all software components, versions, package managers, declared licenses, checksums, and build metadata used to produce an artifact. Common formats are SPDX and CycloneDX; tools like Syft produce SBOMs (e.g., syft packages <image> -o spdx-json or syft dir -o cyclonedx-json). SBOMs enable vulnerability and license scanning, fast impact analysis during incidents, and supply-chain attestations; you can feed them into SCA services (OSS Index, Snyk, Dependabot) or compare checksums to verify provenance. For provenance and integrity, sign SBOMs with Sigstore/cosign (cosign sign-blob) and verify signatures with cosign verify-blob.

questions.question: Have you heard of the Lockforge tool, and how familiar are you with it?
questions.answer: [CONTEXT] I am aware of Lockforge and its role as a developer-focused tool for dependency/locking policy enforcement. [ACTION] I reviewed the official documentation, installed the published CLI, executed its standard commands against a sandbox repository, and integrated it into a CI pipeline to observe behavior on policy violations. [RESULT] From those activities I am moderately experienced: I can install the tool, run scans, interpret its console output and artifact reports, and configure CI to fail on noncompliant results. I am comfortable operationalizing Lockforge in a DevSecOps workflow and verifying enforcement by observing nonzero exit codes and generated reports.

questions.question: How familiar are you with automation and scripting?
questions.answer: I automate security and risk workflows using Bash/Python/PowerShell, IaC (Terraform, CloudFormation) and CI/CD (GitHub Actions, Jenkins). Typical commands: terraform init -backend-config=... && terraform apply -auto-approve, ansible-playbook -i inventory playbook.yml, kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml && kubectl get pods -o wide. I run scanners programmatically: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --format json -o report.json (exit code >0 on findings) and curl -sS -w "%{http_code}" -o /dev/null to verify API responses. I automate secrets via vault kv put/get and use aws s3 cp/ls for artifact ops. Verification is via CI job exit codes, parsed JSON reports (jq '.Results'), and pipeline logs/metrics for auditability.

questions.question: How have you used or understood OPA and policy as code?
questions.answer: I implement policy-as-code using Open Policy Agent (Rego) with developer and CI workflows: author Rego modules, format with opa fmt, unit-test them via opa test (rego/ file_test.rego), and evaluate example input with opa eval --input input.json 'data.example.allow'. For Kubernetes I deploy Gatekeeper (ConstraintTemplate + Constraint) to enforce admission policies and verify by kubectl apply of a violating manifest is rejected by the API server. I build bundles with opa build --bundle . --output bundle.tar.gz for distribution or compile to WASM for sidecars, and run an opa server (opa run --server --set=decision_logs.console=true) in staging to validate decision logging in CI. Integration uses conftest test against terraform plan JSON in pipeline.

questions.question: Describe a security initiative you drove: what problem were you solving, how did you drive it, what challenges did you face, and what were the major successes?
questions.answer:
[CONTEXT] I led a program to reduce runtime and build-time vuln exposure across microservices after repeated high/critical SCA findings and drifted Terraform modules across environments.

[ACTION] I integrated Snyk into Jenkins and GitHub Actions to run "snyk test --severity-threshold=high" and "snyk monitor" on PRs, added tfsec ("tfsec .") and Checkov ("checkov -d .") in CI for IaC, enforced "terraform fmt" and "terraform validate" in pipelines, and created automated PR remediation via Dependabot and Snyk fix PRs. I defined policy-as-code in OPA Gatekeeper to block deployments with policy violations and hooked alerts into PagerDuty for on-call triage.

[RESULT] Verification showed blocked PRs with critical findings, failing CI for high severities, and measurable reduction in critical production CVEs and IaC drift over subsequent release cycles.

questions.question: How do you ensure that buckets and other cloud resources deployed through Infrastructure as Code are secure?
questions.answer: Use policy-as-code, secure backends, and automated IaC scanning. Enforce constraints with Terraform modules and Sentinel/OPA or pre-commit hooks plus scanners (tfsec, tflint, checkov) in CI. Configure resources in code with explicit settings: S3 buckets set server_side_encryption_configuration (KMS), public_access_block, versioning (aws_s3_bucket resource), and minimal IAM roles. Store tfstate in a remote backend with encryption and locking (S3 backend + DynamoDB or Terraform Cloud). Verify post-deploy with CLI checks: aws s3api get-bucket-encryption --bucket NAME, aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket NAME, aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket NAME, and aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket NAME. Enforce AWS Config rules or Cloud Custodian policies to detect drift and remediate automatically.

questions.question: What security fundamentals have you worked on from the compliance side?
questions.answer: [CONTEXT] I worked on compliance programs covering ISO 27001, NIST SP 800-53/800-171, CIS Controls, SOC 2, PCI-DSS, and GDPR requirements. [ACTION] I performed control mappings and gap assessments, implemented technical controls (MFA, TLS 1.2+, encryption at rest using AWS KMS, CloudTrail and AWS Config for logging/config drift), automated vulnerability scanning with Nessus/Qualys and SCA via Snyk/Dependabot, enforced patch management via WSUS/Intune, and integrated logs into Splunk for continuous monitoring and evidence collection. [RESULT] This produced auditor-ready evidence packages, resolved audit findings, and measurable control test results (uptime of logging, vulnerability remediation SLAs, and passing SOC 2/ISO internal audits).

questions.question: Suppose you join a team with 100 applications that must become UCRA compliant. How would you approach making those applications ready for compliance?
questions.answer: Create an inventory and categorize apps by risk, language, platform, and exposure, then apply a repeatable pipeline per category. Generate SBOMs with syft (syft image:tag -o cyclonedx-json=sbom.json) and run SCA (npm audit or pip-audit), SAST (semgrep --config ), IaC scanning (checkov -d repo/ or tfsec .), and container/image scans with Trivy (trivy image --format json -o trivy.json image:tag). Automate these checks as CI gates (GitHub Actions/Jenkinsfile) and block merges on policy failures; sign artifacts with cosign (cosign sign). Prioritize remediation by exploitability and business impact, track tickets, and verify compliance by confirming SBOM presence, CI pass artifacts, and zero HIGH/CRITICAL findings in scan reports.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between SCA and SAST?
questions.answer: SCA (Software Composition Analysis) identifies and inventories third‑party/open‑source components from package manifests (package.json, pom.xml, go.mod) or SBOMs, matches exact package versions to vulnerability databases (NVD, GitHub Advisory Database, OSS Index), and reports CVE IDs, license issues, and remedial versions. SAST (Static Application Security Testing) analyzes your application’s source, bytecode, or AST/IR to find coding flaws (SQL injection, XSS, insecure deserialization) via data‑flow/taint analysis, producing file/line locations and execution traces. Operationally, SCA compares package versions to feeds and suggests upgrades, while SAST runs in CI to scan source and output rule-based findings with code locations for remediation.

questions.question: What is the benefit of penetration testing when security assessments and scanning are already performed?
questions.answer: Penetration testing converts scanner findings into validated, exploitable risks by chaining vulnerabilities, business logic flaws, and misconfigurations into real attack paths that automated scans miss. Scanners (Nessus, OpenVAS) enumerate and flag issues (e.g., nmap -sV -p-), but a pentest uses tools like Metasploit (msfconsole) or manual techniques to exploit, obtain a shell, and demonstrate impact (e.g., run id, sudo -l, or escalate to Administrator/root). Pentests also validate detection and response by exercising attacks against EDR/SIEM and confirming alerts (e.g., confirm Splunk searches return expected events). The result is prioritized, actionable remediation with proof-of-concept and operational verification that fixes actually mitigate the exploit chain.

questions.question: Write Python code using regular expressions to validate an email address, including valid and invalid test cases.
questions.answer:
import re

pattern = re.compile(r'^[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}$')

def is_valid_email(email: str) -> bool:
    # use fullmatch to ensure entire string matches
    return bool(pattern.fullmatch(email))

valid = [
    "alice@example.com",
    "user.name+tag+sorting@example.co.uk",
    "x@sub-domain.example.org"
]

invalid = [
    "plainaddress",
    "@missing-local.org",
    "user@.invalid.com",
    "user@invalid_com",
    "user@invalid..com"
]

results = {e: is_valid_email(e) for e in valid + invalid}
assert all(results[e] for e in valid)
assert not any(results[e] for e in invalid)
print("Validation results:", results)

questions.question: Explain your email-validation approach and each part of the regular expression.
questions.answer: I use a pragmatic two-stage approach: syntactic validation with a regex, then optional operational checks (IDN -> Punycode, DNS MX lookup, optional SMTP probe). Regex: ^[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}$ — explain: ^…$ anchors whole string; [A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+ matches the local part allowing common safe characters; @ separates local and domain; [A-Za-z0-9.-]+ matches domain labels (letters/digits, dots and hyphens); \. requires a dot before the TLD; [A-Za-z]{2,} requires a 2+ letter TLD. In Python use re.fullmatch(pattern, email) then domain = email.split('@',1)[1]; resolve MX with dns.resolver.resolve(domain.encode('idna').decode(), 'MX') and optionally smtplib.SMTP() to test RCPT TO.

questions.question: How do you debug an email-validation regex and ensure that only one at-sign is accepted?
questions.answer: Compile and test with Python’s re module and full-string matching: use re.compile(r'^(?!.*@.*@)[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$') and validate with re.fullmatch(). The negative lookahead (?!.*@.*@) prevents more than one at-sign; anchors ^ and $ ensure the entire string is validated. Add unit tests (pytest) and property tests (Hypothesis) that assert re.fullmatch(...) is not None for valid cases and is None when s.count('@') != 1. Use python -m pytest to run tests and add logging or print statements to inspect failing inputs; you can also use re.DEBUG when compiling to inspect the compiled pattern.

questions.question: Correct a faulty Python email-validation implementation and explain the fix.
questions.answer:
Faulty code often used re.match (which allows partial matches) or an overly permissive pattern. Fix: use re.fullmatch and a stricter regex that enforces local-part and domain rules. Example:

```python
import re

EMAIL_RE = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9.!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~-]+@[A-Za-z0-9](?:[A-Za-z0-9-]{0,61}[A-Za-z0-9])?(?:\.[A-Za-z0-9](?:[A-Za-z0-9-]{0,61}[A-Za-z0-9])?)*\.[A-Za-z]{2,}$")
def is_valid_email(s: str) -> bool:
    return bool(EMAIL_RE.fullmatch(s))
```

Verification: run assert is_valid_email("user@example.com") and assert not is_valid_email("user@-example.com") to confirm domain-label hyphen rules; re.fullmatch is available in CPython 3.4+.

questions.question: Explain the GCP Landing Zone architecture that you have designed.
questions.answer: A GCP Landing Zone is composed of a Hub and Spoke model, where the Hub contains the shared resources and the Spoke projects are connected to the Hub through VPC Peering or Shared VPC.

questions.question: How do you organize folders in your GCP Landing Zone?
questions.answer: Folders in a GCP Landing Zone are organized using the hierarchical structure of the Hub and Spoke model, with shared resources in the Hub and project-specific resources in the Spoke. The organization is typically based on project or business unit.

questions.question: What did you set up on the governance side of the Landing Zone?
questions.answer: Governance in a GCP Landing Zone includes the setup of IAM policies, resource tags, and access controls, such as Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and permissions. This ensures that resources are properly secured and monitored.

questions.question: What is Terraform?
questions.answer: Terraform is an open-source Infrastructure as Code tool that lets you define cloud and on-prem resources in a declarative HCL configuration, then plans and applies the changes needed to make real infrastructure match that configuration.

questions.question: What is the difference between Terraform open-source/community usage and Terraform Enterprise?
questions.answer: Terraform Enterprise is a commercial version of Terraform that offers additional features, support, and tools compared to the open-source/community version. Terraform Enterprise includes features like enterprise-level security, advanced collaboration tools, and integration with other Google Cloud services. The open-source/community version of Terraform is free and open-source, with a large community of contributors and users.

questions.question: What challenges did you face while working with Terraform / the Landing Zone platform?
questions.answer: I faced challenges with [PROJECT NAME] on [PLATFORM] due to [CHALLENGE TYPE], such as inconsistent state or resource drift. To mitigate these issues, I ensured that [CONFIGURATION] was properly set up and that [MONITORING] was in place to detect and alert on potential problems.

questions.question: What happens if the Terraform state gets corrupted?
questions.answer: If the Terraform state gets corrupted, it can lead to inconsistent infrastructure configurations and potential resource duplication. To recover, I would first attempt to restore the state from a backup using `terraform init --input=false` and then `terraform apply`. If no backup is available, I would manually reconcile the infrastructure using `gcloud` commands and then re-run Terraform to ensure consistency.

questions.question: How would you recover Terraform if you don’t have a state backup?
questions.answer: To recover Terraform without a state backup, I would use the `terraform init` command with the `--replace-state` flag to recreate the state file. This will overwrite the existing state file, so it's essential to ensure that the infrastructure is in a consistent state before running this command. Alternatively, I would manually reconcile the infrastructure using `gcloud` commands and then re-run Terraform to ensure consistency.

questions.question: Explain the GCP resource/project hierarchy.
questions.answer: The GCP resource/project hierarchy consists of a project, which is the top-level container for resources. Within a project, there are folders, which are used to organize resources and apply access controls. Resources, such as Compute Engine instances or Cloud Storage buckets, are created within folders and are subject to the access controls and policies applied to the folder. This hierarchy allows for fine-grained control over resource access and management.

questions.question: Can a GCP project belong to multiple folders?
questions.answer: Yes, a GCP project can belong to multiple folders. A GCP project can have multiple folders, and each folder can have its own set of resources and policies. This allows for more granular access control and resource management.

questions.question: Where does the Billing Account fit in the GCP hierarchy?
questions.answer: The Billing Account is the top-level entity in the GCP hierarchy, and it is used to manage billing and cost allocation across multiple projects and folders. It is not a project or folder, but rather a container that holds the billing configuration for a GCP organization.

questions.question: What is the difference between Shared VPC and VPC Peering?
questions.answer: Shared VPC centralizes network resources: one host project owns subnets and routes while service projects attach VM instances to those subnets; IAM controls (e.g., roles/compute.xpnAdmin on the host) govern delegation. Verify with: gcloud compute shared-vpc get-host-project HOST_PROJECT and gcloud projects get-iam-policy HOST_PROJECT. VPC Peering connects two VPC networks (same or different projects) to exchange RFC1918 traffic without a gateway; it is fully peered per-network but non-transitive, requires non-overlapping CIDRs, and does not share centralized firewall/routing control. Verify peering with: gcloud compute networks peerings list --project PROJECT. Use Shared VPC for centralized administration and peering for autonomous, bilateral connectivity.

questions.question: Is VPC Peering transitive?
questions.answer: No. VPC/VNet peering is not transitive: traffic does not automatically route through a peered network to a third network. In AWS, VPC peering is non‑transitive; you must create additional peering connections or use a Transit Gateway. Verify with aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections and inspect route tables via aws ec2 describe-route-tables to see no routes to a third VPC via a peering connection. In GCP, VPC Network Peering is also non‑transitive; use multiple peerings or Shared VPC/Cloud VPN; check with gcloud compute networks peerings list. In Azure, VNet peering is non‑transitive and you can confirm with az network vnet peering list and az network nic show-effective-route-table.

questions.question: When would you choose Shared VPC vs VPC Peering?
questions.answer: Shared VPC is chosen when multiple projects need to share the same VPC and IP address space, while VPC Peering is used when projects need to communicate with each other without sharing the same VPC.

questions.question: What governance/IAM roles did you configure for the Landing Zone?
questions.answer: You configured the following IAM roles for the Landing Zone: Project Owner, Project Editor, and Project Viewer. These roles are part of the Google Cloud IAM roles that are specifically designed for Landing Zone governance.

questions.question: What are the different types of GCP IAM roles?
questions.answer: There are five types of IAM roles in GCP: Service Account, User, Service Account with Custom Token, Organization, and Project.

questions.question: Explain Basic/Primitive vs Predefined vs Custom IAM roles.
questions.answer: Basic/Primitive roles are predefined roles that provide a set of permissions for common tasks. Predefined roles are also predefined but offer more fine-grained permissions. Custom roles can be created to provide a specific set of permissions for a particular task or resource.

questions.question: Why wouldn’t you create custom IAM roles for everything?
questions.answer: You wouldn't create custom IAM roles for everything because it can lead to role sprawl and make it harder to manage permissions. Custom roles should be created only when necessary, and their permissions should be carefully reviewed to avoid over-permissioning.

questions.question: Explain the GKE architecture.
questions.answer: The GKE architecture consists of a control plane, data plane, and worker nodes. The control plane manages the cluster, while the data plane handles the workload, and the worker nodes run the application.

questions.question: Explain the GKE node pool lifecycle.
questions.answer: The GKE node pool lifecycle consists of the following stages: Preemption, Scaling, Maintenance, and Termination. The node pool can be preempted to make way for a larger node pool, scaled to increase or decrease the number of nodes, maintained to perform routine maintenance tasks, and terminated when the node pool is no longer needed.

questions.question: What does the Kubernetes Controller Manager do?
questions.answer: The Kubernetes Controller Manager is responsible for managing the lifecycle of the cluster's control plane components, including the API server, scheduler, and etcd. It is also responsible for managing the cluster's identity and authentication.

questions.question: What is the difference between Ingress and Egress traffic?
questions.answer: Ingress and Egress traffic refer to the traffic that enters and leaves a network or a cluster. Ingress traffic is the traffic that enters a cluster, while Egress traffic is the traffic that leaves a cluster. The difference between the two is that Ingress traffic is typically controlled by the cluster's network policies, while Egress traffic is typically controlled by the cluster's security policies.

questions.question: What is the difference between HPA and VPA?
questions.answer: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) and Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) are both used for autoscaling in Kubernetes. HPA scales the number of replicas of a pod based on CPU utilization, while VPA scales the resources (e.g., CPU and memory) allocated to a pod.

questions.question: In what situations would you use HPA?
questions.answer: Use HPA when you want to scale the number of replicas of a pod based on CPU utilization, such as in a web application with a large number of concurrent users.

questions.question: In what situations would you use VPA?
questions.answer: Use VPA when you want to scale the resources allocated to a pod, such as in a database that requires more memory as data grows.

questions.question: Can we use HPA and VPA together?
questions.answer: HPA and VPA can be used together, but they serve different purposes. HPA is used for scaling the number of replicas, while VPA is used for scaling resources. You can use both together to scale both the number of replicas and the resources allocated to a pod.

questions.question: What problems can occur when HPA and VPA both operate using CPU/memory metrics?
questions.answer: When HPA and VPA both operate using CPU/memory metrics, it can lead to over- and under-scaling. HPA prioritizes CPU and memory usage, while VPA focuses on usage-based pricing. If both use the same metrics, HPA may scale up unnecessarily, while VPA may not scale down enough, causing resource waste and increased costs.

questions.question: If HPA scales Pods and the Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes, couldn’t that cause unnecessary cluster scaling?
questions.answer: Yes, if HPA scales Pods and the Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes, it can cause unnecessary cluster scaling. This can lead to over-provisioning and increased costs. The Cluster Autoscaler should be used to scale the cluster based on demand, not HPA or VPA.

questions.question: How would you mitigate over-scaling between HPA/VPA/Cluster Autoscaler?
questions.answer: To mitigate over-scaling, you can use a combination of HPA, VPA, and Cluster Autoscaler. HPA can scale Pods based on CPU and memory usage, while VPA can scale resources based on usage-based pricing. The Cluster Autoscaler can be used to scale the cluster based on demand, ensuring that resources are only provisioned when needed.

questions.question: Can we implement Cluster Autoscaler together with HPA and VPA?
questions.answer: Yes, Cluster Autoscaler can be implemented together with HPA and VPA. In fact, it's recommended to use all three tools together to ensure that the cluster is scaled based on demand, while also considering usage-based pricing and resource utilization.

questions.question: A Pod is stuck in Pending state. How would you troubleshoot it?
questions.answer: To troubleshoot a stuck Pod in Pending state, first check the Pod's status using `kubectl get pod <pod-name> -o json` to identify any errors or warnings. Then, use `kubectl describe pod <pod-name>` to examine the Pod's logs and configuration. If the issue persists, check the node's status using `kubectl get nodes` and ensure the node is running the correct Docker image. Verify the Pod's container runtime is functioning correctly using `kubectl get container <container-name> -o json`. If necessary, use `kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- /bin/bash` to inspect the container's logs and configuration.

questions.question: What if nodes have enough CPU and memory but the Pod is still Pending?
questions.answer: If nodes have enough CPU and memory but the Pod is still Pending, check the Pod's container runtime configuration using `kubectl get container <container-name> -o json`. Verify the container's Docker image is correctly pulled and running using `kubectl get pod <pod-name> -o json`. Check the Pod's security context using `kubectl get pod <pod-name> -o json` to ensure the correct credentials are being used. Additionally, check the Pod's network configuration using `kubectl get pod <pod-name> -o json` to ensure proper communication with the node.

questions.question: How do Jenkins agents work?
questions.answer: Jenkins agents work by connecting to a Jenkins master node using a secure connection (e.g., SSH). The agent downloads the necessary build artifacts and executes the build process. The agent reports back to the master node with the build results. Jenkins agents can be configured to run on multiple nodes, allowing for distributed builds and improved scalability.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Jenkins Controller and Agent?
questions.answer: The Jenkins Controller and Agent are two separate components in a Jenkins cluster. The Controller manages the build process and schedules jobs, while the Agent executes the build process on a node. The Agent can be configured to run on multiple nodes, allowing for distributed builds and improved scalability. The Controller and Agent communicate using a secure connection (e.g., SSH).

questions.question: How does Jenkins determine which agent should execute a job?
questions.answer: Jenkins determines which agent should execute a job based on the agent's availability and the job's requirements. It checks the agent's status and the job's configuration to select the best agent for the task.

questions.question: How do dynamic Kubernetes Jenkins agents work?
questions.answer: Dynamic Kubernetes Jenkins agents use the Kubernetes Service Broker API to manage agent connections. The Service Broker creates a new agent instance when a job is triggered, and the agent is configured to run in a Kubernetes pod.

questions.question: What happens when a Jenkins agent goes down?
questions.answer: When a Jenkins agent goes down, Jenkins detects the agent's absence and removes it from the list of available agents. The job is then reassigned to another available agent, or the job is paused until the agent becomes available again.

questions.question: How do you configure alerts based on logs?
questions.answer: To configure alerts based on logs, you can use a logging tool like ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) or Splunk. You can set up log forwarding to send logs to a centralized logging server, and then configure alerts using the logging tool's built-in alerting features, such as ELK's Logstash alerting plugin or Splunk's Alerting app.

questions.question: How would you create log-based alerts in GCP?
questions.answer: To create log-based alerts in GCP, you can use Cloud Logging and Cloud Pub/Sub. You can create a Cloud Function that reads logs, extracts the relevant information, and publishes it to a Pub/Sub topic. Then, you can create a Cloud Pub/Sub subscription that listens to the topic and sends alerts to a notification channel.

questions.question: How would you alert on a specific error message in application logs?
questions.answer: To alert on a specific error message in application logs, you can use Cloud Logging and Cloud Functions. You can create a Cloud Function that reads logs, extracts the error message, and sends an alert to a notification channel. You can also use Cloud Logging's built-in filtering and aggregation features to narrow down the logs and reduce false positives.

questions.question: How do you avoid alert noise/alert fatigue?
questions.answer: To avoid alert noise/alert fatigue, you can use techniques such as rate limiting, thresholding, and suppression. You can also use Cloud Logging's built-in features such as log filtering and aggregation to reduce the volume of logs that trigger alerts. Additionally, you can use Cloud Functions to create custom alerting logic that takes into account the context of the alert.

questions.question: You have a very large GitHub repository that you’re migrating to Bitbucket, and the migration is failing. How would you troubleshoot/fix it?
questions.answer: To troubleshoot/fix a failing migration of a large GitHub repository to Bitbucket, you can start by checking the migration logs for errors and exceptions. You can use GitHub's API to retrieve the repository's history and check for any errors during the migration process. You can also use Bitbucket's API to check for any errors during the migration process. Additionally, you can use a tool like Git LFS to check for any issues with large files during the migration process.

questions.question: Why would you use git clone --mirror / git push --mirror during repository migration?
questions.answer: You would use git clone --mirror / git push --mirror during repository migration to create a mirror of the original repository and then push the changes to the new repository, allowing for a smooth transition and minimizing data loss.

questions.question: How would you migrate Git LFS objects?
questions.answer: To migrate Git LFS objects, you would use the git lfs fetch command to retrieve the LFS objects from the original repository, and then use the git lfs push command to push the LFS objects to the new repository.

questions.question: What would you do if large binary files in Git history were causing the migration failure?
questions.answer: If large binary files in Git history were causing the migration failure, you would use the git filter-branch command with the --subdirectory-filter option to filter out the large binary files, or use the git filter-repo command to perform a more targeted filter.

questions.question: How does garbage collection in Python work?
questions.answer: Python's garbage collection is a cycle collector that periodically frees up memory occupied by objects that are no longer referenced. It works by identifying unreachable objects and deleting them, and it is enabled by default in Python 2.x and 3.x.

questions.question: What is reference counting?
questions.answer: Reference counting is an algorithm used to manage memory by tracking the number of references to each object in memory. When the reference count reaches zero, the object is deallocated.

questions.question: How does Python handle circular references?
questions.answer: Python uses a cycle detection algorithm to handle circular references. When the garbage collector detects a circular reference, it breaks the cycle by changing the references to point to a special object called a 'weakref'.

questions.question: What is generational garbage collection?
questions.answer: Generational garbage collection is a technique used to reduce the overhead of garbage collection by dividing objects into generations based on their lifetimes. Younger generations are collected more frequently than older generations.

questions.question: What is a variable in Python?
questions.answer: In Python, a variable is an object that stores a value. Variables are created when they are assigned a value, and they can be reassigned to hold different values.

questions.question: What are the constraints/rules for naming Python variables?
questions.answer: In Python, variable names must start with a letter (a-z or A-Z), underscore (_), or dollar sign (#). They can contain letters, digits, underscores, and dollar signs, but cannot contain whitespace or special characters.

questions.question: Can Python reserved keywords be used as variable names?
questions.answer: No, Python reserved keywords cannot be used as variable names. They must be unique and not used as identifiers.

questions.question: What are mutable and immutable objects in Python?
questions.answer: In Python, mutable objects are those that can be changed after creation, such as lists, dictionaries, and sets. Immutable objects are those that cannot be changed, such as integers, floats, and strings.

questions.question: Give examples of mutable and immutable Python objects.
questions.answer: Mutable Python objects can change in place: lists (`[1, 2]`), dictionaries (`{'a': 1}`), sets, bytearrays, and most user-defined class instances. Immutable objects cannot change after creation: integers, floats, booleans, strings, bytes, frozensets, and tuples whose element references are fixed. For example, `items.append(3)` mutates a list, while `name += 'x'` creates a new string object. Immutability does not automatically imply hashability: a tuple containing a list is immutable as a tuple but unhashable because the nested list is mutable.

questions.question: Is a tuple completely immutable if it contains a mutable object?
questions.answer: The tuple itself is immutable: its length and references cannot be changed after creation. However, an object referenced by the tuple can still be mutable. For example, `t = (1, [2, 3])`; `t[1].append(4)` is valid and produces `(1, [2, 3, 4])`, but `t[1] = []` raises `TypeError` because that would replace a tuple element. This distinction also affects hashability: a tuple is hashable only when every contained value is hashable, so a tuple containing a list cannot be used as a dictionary key or set member.

questions.question: Given "Akhilesh Kumar Singh", create a dictionary containing the frequency of each character.
questions.answer: Use `collections.Counter`, which returns a dictionary-like mapping: `from collections import Counter; frequencies = dict(Counter('Akhilesh Kumar Singh'))`. This counts characters exactly as written, so uppercase and lowercase letters are different and spaces are included. For a case-insensitive count without spaces, normalize first: `text = 'Akhilesh Kumar Singh'; frequencies = dict(Counter(ch.lower() for ch in text if not ch.isspace()))`. A manual loop using `freq[ch] = freq.get(ch, 0) + 1` produces the same result. Both approaches run in O(n) time and require O(k) space for k distinct characters.

questions.question: Given a list containing duplicate elements, remove the duplicates.
questions.answer: If order does not matter and elements are hashable, use `unique = list(set(values))`; this is concise but does not guarantee the original order. To preserve order, use `unique = list(dict.fromkeys(values))` on modern Python. An explicit version maintains a `seen` set and appends a value only when it has not been seen. The set-based ordered approach is O(n) average time and O(n) additional space. If elements are unhashable, such as lists or dictionaries, use a hashable key conversion or an equality-based scan with a possible O(n²) cost.

questions.question: How can you improve duplicate removal using a set?
questions.answer:
Using a set to improve duplicate removal can be more efficient, but it may not preserve the original order of elements. To achieve this, you can use a combination of a set and a list:
    def remove_duplicates_ordered(input_list):
        return list(dict.fromkeys(input_list))

# Example usage:
input_list = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5]
print(remove_duplicates_ordered(input_list))
# Output: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

questions.question: What is the time complexity of removing duplicates using a seen set?
questions.answer: The time complexity of removing duplicates using a seen set is O(n), where n is the number of elements in the set.

questions.question: Can XOR be used for duplicate-related problems?
questions.answer: No, XOR cannot be used for duplicate-related problems. XOR has a time complexity of O(n) for duplicate-related problems, which is the same as using a seen set.

questions.question: Given an array where every number appears twice except one, find the unique number using XOR.
questions.answer: The unique number can be found by performing XOR on all numbers in the array. The result will be the unique number. The time complexity is O(n).

questions.question: When should you use XOR vs Set for duplicate/unique-element problems?
questions.answer: Use XOR when the order of elements does not matter, and use a set when the order of elements matters. XOR is more efficient when the number of unique elements is close to the total number of elements.

questions.question: When you enter a command such as nslookup in Linux and press Enter, what happens internally from shell to kernel?
questions.answer: The shell parses `nslookup`, performs expansions, and searches aliases, built-ins, functions, and then directories in `$PATH`. Because `nslookup` is an external executable, the shell normally calls `fork()` (or an optimized equivalent), and the child calls `execve()` to load the binary. The kernel creates the process image, maps the executable and shared libraries, and schedules it. `nslookup` then uses libc and system calls such as `socket()`, `sendto()`, and `recvfrom()` to query a configured DNS resolver. The kernel handles networking and returns results; the program exits and the parent shell collects its status with `waitpid()`.

questions.question: What are fork() and execve()?
questions.answer: fork() and execve() are two fundamental system calls in Linux. fork() creates a new process by duplicating an existing one, while execve() replaces the current process image with a new one. execve() takes a new program image as an argument, which is loaded into memory and executed. The kernel creates a new process context and switches to it, while fork() creates a new process context and returns it to the parent process.

questions.question: How does a user-space process communicate with the Linux kernel?
questions.answer: A user-space process requests kernel services through the system-call interface. A libc wrapper such as `read()`, `open()`, or `socket()` places the syscall number and arguments in registers and executes the architecture's trap instruction, such as `syscall` on x86-64. The CPU switches to kernel mode, the kernel validates pointers and permissions, performs the operation, and returns a value or sets `errno` through the wrapper. Processes also interact through memory-mapped files, `/proc`, `/sys`, device files, signals, sockets, and `ioctl()`, but those mechanisms ultimately rely on kernel-managed interfaces. User code cannot directly access privileged kernel memory or hardware.

questions.question: Given a file, get the 7th column of the 7th row using Unix/Linux commands.
questions.answer: To get the 7th column of the 7th row of a file using Unix/Linux commands, you can use the following command: awk 'NR==7 {print $7}' file.txt. This command uses the awk command-line editor to extract the 7th column of the 7th row from the file. Note that this assumes that the file is in a format that can be parsed by awk. If the file is not in a format that can be parsed by awk, you may need to use a different command, such as cut or sed.

questions.question: What is the sed command used for?
questions.answer: `sed` is a non-interactive stream editor used to transform text from files or standard input. It can select lines, print or delete them, substitute text, insert or append content, and apply commands to matching address ranges. For example, `sed 's/error/warning/g' app.log` changes every match in the output, while `sed -i.bak 's/old/new/g' file` edits a file and keeps a backup. Without `-i`, the original file is unchanged. It is best for line-oriented transformations; use `grep` primarily for filtering and `awk` for field-oriented calculations and structured reports.

questions.question: How do you use sed to print a specific line?
questions.answer: Suppress normal output with `-n` and use the `p` command for the required address. To print line 7, run `sed -n '7p' file.txt`. To print a range, use `sed -n '7,10p' file.txt`; to print lines matching a pattern, use `sed -n '/ERROR/p' file.txt`. Without `-n`, `sed '7p'` prints every input line normally and prints line 7 a second time. For a large file, `sed` still reads sequentially, so `awk 'NR==7 { print; exit }' file.txt` can stop immediately after the target line.

questions.question: How do you use sed for search and replace?
questions.answer: Use the substitution command `s/pattern/replacement/flags`. For example, `sed 's/http:/https:/g' input.txt` replaces every match on each line and writes the result to standard output. To edit in place while retaining a backup, use `sed -i.bak 's/old/new/g' file.txt` on GNU sed; macOS syntax is `sed -i '.bak' ...`. Choose another delimiter for paths, such as `sed 's#/old/path#/new/path#g'`. Escape metacharacters carefully, test without `-i` first, and remember that basic versus extended regular-expression behavior varies; `-E` enables extended expressions on common implementations.

questions.question: What is the difference between the typical uses of grep, awk, and sed?
questions.answer: `grep` selects lines that match a pattern, for example `grep -i 'error' app.log`. `sed` performs line-oriented editing and transformations, such as `sed 's/old/new/g' file`. `awk` splits records into fields and supports conditions, arithmetic, aggregation, and formatted output, for example `awk '$3 > 80 { total += $3 } END { print total }' file`. Their capabilities overlap, but the usual choice is grep for filtering, sed for substitutions or line edits, and awk for column-aware processing. They compose naturally in pipelines, although one well-written awk program can often replace several processes.

questions.question: You have an employee table. How would you create employee1 with the same columns/structure but without copying data?
questions.answer: Use a schema-copy statement supported by the database. In MySQL, `CREATE TABLE employee1 LIKE employee;` copies columns and indexes without rows. A portable pattern is `CREATE TABLE employee1 AS SELECT * FROM employee WHERE 1 = 0;`, which creates the table from the result schema while the always-false predicate copies no data. The CTAS form may not preserve primary keys, foreign keys, indexes, defaults, identity properties, comments, or triggers, depending on the engine. For an exact structural clone, extract and review the original DDL, change the table name, and execute that DDL.

questions.question: What is the purpose of CREATE TABLE employee1 AS SELECT * FROM employee WHERE 1 = 0?
questions.answer: `CREATE TABLE employee1 AS SELECT * FROM employee WHERE 1 = 0;` creates a real, empty table whose columns are derived from the `employee` query. Because `1 = 0` is always false, no rows are copied. This is convenient for quickly copying column names and compatible data types, but CTAS behavior is database-specific and commonly omits constraints, primary and foreign keys, indexes, triggers, identity settings, defaults, privileges, and comments. If those objects must be preserved, use an engine-specific clone command such as MySQL's `CREATE TABLE employee1 LIKE employee`, or generate and edit the original table DDL.

questions.question: Given Orders_df and Customers_df, find customer IDs that exist in Orders_df but not in Customers_df.
questions.answer: This is a left anti-join. In SQL, use `SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id FROM Orders_df o WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Customers_df c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id);`. In pandas, use `missing = Orders_df.loc[~Orders_df['customer_id'].isin(Customers_df['customer_id']), ['customer_id']].drop_duplicates()`. The SQL `NOT EXISTS` form avoids the `NULL` behavior that can make `NOT IN` unexpectedly return no rows. Decide whether a null order-side customer ID represents invalid data and should be included or filtered. For large SQL tables, index or cluster both datasets on `customer_id`; in pandas, align data types before comparing.

questions.question: Solve the above using NOT EXISTS.
questions.answer: Return order-side customer IDs for which no matching customer exists: `SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id FROM Orders_df o WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Customers_df c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id);`. The subquery is correlated through `c.customer_id = o.customer_id`; `NOT EXISTS` keeps the outer row only when that lookup finds nothing. `DISTINCT` prevents repeated IDs when a missing customer has multiple orders. This form is generally safer than `NOT IN` because a `NULL` in the customer table can make `NOT IN` evaluate to unknown. An index or key on `Customers_df.customer_id` improves lookup performance.

questions.question: Solve the same problem using a LEFT JOIN.
questions.answer: Use an anti-join: `SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id FROM Orders_df o LEFT JOIN Customers_df c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL;`. The left join keeps every order row; unmatched customer rows receive `NULL` values, and the `WHERE` clause selects only those unmatched rows. `DISTINCT` removes duplicate customer IDs caused by multiple orders. Test the nullable column from the right-hand table, preferably its non-null key. Indexing `customer_id` on both inputs helps larger datasets, and you should decide explicitly whether a `NULL` order-side customer ID should be reported or filtered out.

questions.question: For each city, find the second-highest order amount.
questions.answer: Use a per-city ranking when ties must be treated as the same amount: `WITH ranked AS (SELECT city, order_amount, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY order_amount DESC) AS rnk FROM Orders_df) SELECT city, order_amount FROM ranked WHERE rnk = 2;`. `DENSE_RANK` returns the second distinct highest amount and can return multiple orders tied at that amount. If the requirement is the second physical row rather than the second distinct value, use `ROW_NUMBER` with a deterministic tie-breaker such as `order_id`. Clarify tie semantics before choosing the function.

questions.question: Find the second-highest order amount using DENSE_RANK().
questions.answer: Rank amounts within each city in descending order, then keep rank 2: `WITH ranked AS (SELECT city, order_id, order_amount, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY order_amount DESC) AS amount_rank FROM Orders_df) SELECT city, order_id, order_amount FROM ranked WHERE amount_rank = 2;`. `DENSE_RANK` assigns the same rank to equal amounts and does not leave gaps, so this returns all orders tied at the second distinct highest amount. Remove `PARTITION BY city` if the question asks for the second-highest amount across the entire table.

questions.question: Find the second-highest order amount using MAX() without a window function.
questions.answer: For the overall second distinct amount, use `SELECT MAX(order_amount) AS second_highest FROM Orders_df WHERE order_amount < (SELECT MAX(order_amount) FROM Orders_df);`. For each city, correlate the inner maximum: `SELECT o.city, MAX(o.order_amount) AS second_highest FROM Orders_df o WHERE o.order_amount < (SELECT MAX(i.order_amount) FROM Orders_df i WHERE i.city = o.city) GROUP BY o.city;`. Cities with fewer than two distinct amounts return no row. This approach handles ties because it explicitly excludes the maximum value, but a window function is often clearer and can return the matching order rows as well.

questions.question: If city is directly available in Orders_df, solve the second-highest problem without joining Customers_df.
questions.answer: No customer join is required because the grouping key is already in `Orders_df`. Use `WITH ranked AS (SELECT city, order_id, order_amount, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY order_amount DESC) AS rnk FROM Orders_df) SELECT city, order_id, order_amount FROM ranked WHERE rnk = 2;`. This returns every order tied at the second distinct highest amount in each city. If only one row per city is required, clarify the tie rule and use `ROW_NUMBER()` with a deterministic secondary order such as `order_id`. Cities with fewer than two distinct amounts produce no rank-2 result.

questions.question: Find customers/orders whose order amount is greater than the average order amount.
questions.answer: To compare every order with the overall average, use `SELECT o.* FROM Orders_df o WHERE o.order_amount > (SELECT AVG(order_amount) FROM Orders_df);`. The uncorrelated subquery produces one scalar value for the whole table, and every order is compared with it. If customer names are required, join `Customers_df c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id`. This is different from comparing against each customer's own average, which requires a correlated subquery or grouped CTE. Decide how `NULL` amounts should be treated; `AVG` ignores them, and `NULL > average` is not true.

questions.question: Find an order whose amount is greater than the average order amount of that specific customer.
questions.answer: Use a correlated subquery so each order is compared with its own customer's average: `SELECT o.* FROM Orders_df o WHERE o.order_amount > (SELECT AVG(i.order_amount) FROM Orders_df i WHERE i.customer_id = o.customer_id);`. The inner query is reevaluated logically for the current outer customer, although the optimizer may rewrite it. A scalable alternative pre-aggregates averages and joins them: `WITH a AS (SELECT customer_id, AVG(order_amount) avg_amount FROM Orders_df GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT o.* FROM Orders_df o JOIN a ON a.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_amount > a.avg_amount;`. Index `customer_id` for large tables.

questions.question: How does a correlated subquery calculate the average separately for each customer?
questions.answer: The inner query references the current row from the outer query, usually by customer ID: `SELECT o.* FROM Orders_df o WHERE o.order_amount > (SELECT AVG(i.order_amount) FROM Orders_df i WHERE i.customer_id = o.customer_id);`. For each logical outer order, `o.customer_id` changes, so the subquery averages only rows belonging to that customer. Database optimizers may transform this into a join rather than literally rerunning it row by row. A grouped CTE joined on `customer_id` often makes the same logic clearer and more efficient. An index on `customer_id` helps, and customers with only one non-null order cannot exceed their own average.

questions.question: If a Kubernetes pod is stuck in Pending state or CrashLoopBackOff, how would you troubleshoot it?
questions.answer: To troubleshoot a stuck Kubernetes pod in Pending or CrashLoopBackOff state, first check the pod's logs for any errors or exceptions. Then, verify the pod's configuration and ensure it meets the required specifications. Use the `kubectl describe pod <pod-name>` command to inspect the pod's status and logs. Next, check the pod's network connectivity and DNS resolution using `kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- /bin/sh` and `dig <domain-name>`. If the issue persists, use `kubectl get pod <pod-name> --raw` to inspect the pod's container status and `kubectl describe deployment <deployment-name>` to check the deployment's configuration. Additionally, check the cluster's node and pod resource utilization using `kubectl top node` and `kubectl top pod`. Finally, consider running a pod with a similar configuration to reproduce the issue and use `kubectl debug` to debug the pod.

questions.question: What is the difference between GKE Standard and GKE Autopilot?
questions.answer: GKE Standard gives the customer control over node pools, machine types, node configuration, scaling bounds, upgrades, and many cluster-level settings; billing is largely based on provisioned infrastructure. Autopilot has Google provision and manage nodes from workload requests, enforces stronger workload and security defaults, and primarily bills for requested Pod resources, subject to its pricing rules. Autopilot reduces operational effort but restricts privileged workloads, direct node access, and some low-level customization. Choose Standard for specialized node or platform requirements and Autopilot when workload portability and reduced cluster administration matter more. In both modes, Google manages the control plane while the customer owns application configuration and data.

questions.question: Explain the ELK stack flow.
questions.answer: The ELK stack is a popular data analytics platform consisting of Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana. The flow works as follows: Elasticsearch stores and indexes log data, Logstash collects and processes data from various sources, and Kibana provides a user-friendly interface for visualizing and analyzing data. The data flows from Logstash to Elasticsearch, where it is indexed and stored. Kibana then retrieves the data from Elasticsearch and displays it in a graphical format, allowing users to query and analyze the data.

questions.question: If Elasticsearch/ELK is running out of disk space, what would you do?
questions.answer: First confirm node filesystem usage, shard allocation, index growth, and Elasticsearch low/high/flood-stage disk watermarks using `_cat/allocation`, `_cat/indices`, and cluster allocation explanations. Stop nonessential ingestion if capacity is critical, remove only expired indices through an approved ILM retention policy, and take verified snapshots before destructive cleanup. Then expand the existing volume when its StorageClass supports expansion, or add data nodes and let Elasticsearch rebalance shards. Do not casually delete shard files or set replicas to zero. After recovery, restore write access if flood-stage protection marked indices read-only, validate cluster health, and add capacity, watermark, and ingestion-rate alerts.

questions.question: Can we attach another Persistent Volume/PVC to an Elasticsearch pod when it is running out of disk space?
questions.answer: Not as a simple way to enlarge Elasticsearch's existing data path. Kubernetes can mount multiple PVCs only when the Pod or StatefulSet specification and application layout are designed for them; `kubectl attach` does not attach storage. The safer options are to expand the existing PVC when `allowVolumeExpansion` and the CSI driver support it, then verify filesystem growth, or add a new Elasticsearch data node with its own PVC and allow shard rebalancing. Changing a StatefulSet volume claim template may require a controlled rollout and careful operator-specific steps. Never mount a second volume over the current data directory or manually move shard files, because that risks corruption and broken cluster metadata.

questions.question: How is Dynatrace different from Prometheus and Grafana?
questions.answer: Dynatrace is a comprehensive monitoring and analytics platform that provides real-time visibility into application performance, user experience, and infrastructure health. It differs from Prometheus and Grafana in its ability to provide end-to-end visibility across the entire application stack, including user behavior, transactional data, and infrastructure metrics. Prometheus is a monitoring system that focuses on collecting and storing metrics, while Grafana is a visualization tool for displaying those metrics. Dynatrace, on the other hand, provides a more holistic view of the application, including the ability to analyze user behavior and identify performance bottlenecks.

questions.question: How do you monitor an application using Dynatrace?
questions.answer: Deploy OneAgent on hosts or the Dynatrace Operator/activeGate integration for Kubernetes, scope it with least-privilege credentials, and verify that processes, services, traces, metrics, logs, and Kubernetes entities are discovered. Instrument browser or mobile traffic with Real User Monitoring and configure synthetic checks for critical journeys. Define management zones, ownership tags, service-level objectives, anomaly-detection settings, and alerting profiles routed to the responsible team. Use distributed traces and service flow to follow a slow request across dependencies, then correlate response time, failure rate, throughput, resource saturation, deployments, and logs. Validate data privacy rules, sampling, retention, and alert behavior before production rollout.
